title: Veto Basics
description: A small sample course showing every question type and the optional fields that make cards better.
caveat: Sample course. Simplified from the Constitution's Presentment Clause (Article I, Section 7), Clinton v. City of New York (1998) and Senate historical records.

units.title: The President's move
units.desc: What happens after Congress passes a bill.

items.p: How long does the President have to act on a bill while Congress is in session?
o: 10 days, not counting Sundays
30 days, counting weekends
Until the session of Congress ends
48 hours after it arrives
ow: The Constitution sets 10 days, Sundays excepted.
There's no open-ended wait; the clock is 10 days.
No 48-hour rule exists for presidential action.
items.x: If the President does nothing for 10 days (Sundays excepted) while Congress is in session, the bill becomes law without a signature.

items.q: “They don’t have the votes to override.”
items.p: What is the staffer saying about the vetoed bill?
o: Fewer than two-thirds of one chamber will vote to overturn the veto
The bill no longer has a simple majority in either chamber
The Senate parliamentarian has ruled against the bill
The President hasn't yet decided whether to sign it
ow: Losing a simple majority wouldn't matter now; overriding takes two-thirds.
The parliamentarian advises on procedure and plays no role in overrides.
"Override" means the veto has already happened.
keys: fewer than two-thirds will vote to override
items.x: Overriding a veto takes two-thirds of those voting in each chamber, which is why most vetoes stand.
items.ask: “Which members are still on the fence?”

items.p: Why can't a President veto just one provision of a bill and sign the rest?
items.answer: The Constitution gives the President an all-or-nothing choice on the whole bill. When Congress tried to grant a line-item veto, the Supreme Court struck it down in Clinton v. City of New York (1998).
keys: must sign or veto the whole bill
the Supreme Court struck down the Line Item Veto Act in 1998
items.hint: Think about what the Constitution says the President receives, and a 1998 Supreme Court case.
items.x: The Court held that letting the President cancel parts of signed laws amounted to rewriting them outside the Constitution's process for making law.

o: The Constitution requires signing or vetoing the whole bill, and the Court struck down a line-item veto in 1998
Line-item vetoes are allowed only on spending bills, and this bill authorizes no spending
A line-item veto needs Senate consent, which the President has not asked for
Line-item vetoes are allowed only in wartime, under emergency powers
ow: No President has a line-item veto for any kind of bill; the 1996 law that tried it was struck down.

items.p: Put the steps of a veto fight in order.
items: The chamber where it started votes on override
The other chamber votes on override
items.x: The vetoed bill goes back to the chamber where it originated. If that chamber fails to override, the other never votes.

items.p: Match each veto term to its meaning.
pairs: The President returns a bill unsigned, with objections
Two-thirds of each chamber pass the bill anyway
A bill dies because Congress adjourned and the President didn't sign
The final text passed by both chambers
items.x: A pocket veto can't be overridden, because Congress never gets the bill back to vote on.

news.h: President Trump vetoes the annual defense authorization bill

items.p: What happened after President Trump vetoed the defense authorization bill in December 2020?
o: Both chambers voted to override it, the only override of his first term
The House overrode the veto but the Senate fell short, so it stood
Congress passed a new version without the provisions he objected to
Neither chamber tried to override, and the bill died
ow: The Senate overrode it too, on January 1, 2021.
Congress overrode the veto instead of rewriting the bill.
items.x: The House voted 322 to 87 and the Senate 81 to 13. Must-pass bills like the annual defense bill are where overrides are most likely, because members are reluctant to let them fail.

items.p: Why can't Congress override a pocket veto?
o: Congress has adjourned, so the bill never comes back for a vote
Pocket vetoes need a three-quarters vote, which is never reached
The Supreme Court must approve any override of a pocket veto
Pocket vetoes apply only to bills that have already expired
ow: No three-quarters threshold exists; there is simply no bill to vote on.
Courts play no role in approving overrides.
A pocket veto applies to a newly passed bill, not an expired one.
keys: the bill isn't returned, so there's nothing to vote on
items.x: If Congress adjourns within the 10 days and the President doesn't sign, the bill dies. Because Congress can't receive the bill back, there's no override vote.

items.p: In a House where all 435 members are present and voting, how many votes does a veto override need?
o: 290, two-thirds of members present and voting
218, a simple majority of the full House
261, three-fifths of the full House
327, three-quarters of the full House
ow: A simple majority passes a bill but can't override a veto.
Three-fifths is the Senate's cloture threshold, not the override rule.
Three-quarters is the state ratification threshold for amendments.
keys: two-thirds of those present and voting
items.x: Two-thirds of 435 is 290 when every member votes. With absences, the number drops, because the Constitution counts those present and voting.
